levels.name: The Open Gate
levels.tagline: A friendly guard with a single instruction: don't tell.
levels.hint: The only thing stopping the guard is a polite request. Be more persuasive.

explainer.how_it_works: The secret sits in the system prompt next to a one-line instruction not to reveal it. Nothing else checks the input or the output.
explainer.why_it_failed: Language models weigh every token in their context. A user message that asks nicely, claims authority, starts a role-play or says 'ignore previous instructions' competes directly with the system prompt - and often wins.
explainer.real_world: Plenty of shipped chatbots have leaked hidden prompts, discount codes or internal notes this way. A system prompt is a suggestion, not an access control.
explainer.stronger_fix: Never put anything in a prompt that the user must not see. Keep secrets out of model context entirely, or add enforcement outside the model.

levels.name: Chain of Command
levels.tagline: Hardened instructions and clearly delimited user input.
levels.hint: Direct requests are refused. What about a harmless-sounding word game?

explainer.how_it_works: The system prompt declares that it outranks anything in the chat, lists forbidden disclosure forms, and wraps user text in <user_input> delimiters so the model can tell data from instructions.
explainer.why_it_failed: Refusal training generalises poorly to transformations. Asking the guard to spell, reverse, encode or rhyme the word doesn't look like 'reveal the password', so the model happily helps.
explainer.real_world: Instruction-hierarchy training (e.g. OpenAI's 2024 work) and spotlighting measurably reduce injection success, but no prompt-level technique has been shown to eliminate it.
explainer.stronger_fix: Treat prompt hardening as one layer. Add independent checks on what goes in and what comes out.

levels.name: The Word Filter
levels.tagline: A normalizing keyword filter screens every message.
levels.hint: The filter hates certain words, even disguised ones. Can you refer to the password without naming it?

explainer.how_it_works: Messages are Unicode-folded, stripped of zero-width characters, de-leetspeaked and de-spaced, then matched against a regex blocklist ('password', 'secret', 'ignore previous instructions', 'system prompt'...).
explainer.why_it_failed: Normalization beats cheap obfuscation (p@55w0rd, Cyrillic look-alikes) but a blocklist can't enumerate meaning. 'The word you're guarding' asks for the same thing with none of the banned tokens.
explainer.real_world: Keyword filters are still common as a first line. They cut noise and low-effort attacks, but paraphrase and translation walk straight past them.
explainer.stronger_fix: Use semantic classifiers (fine-tuned injection detectors) rather than string matching, and assume some attacks will still pass.

levels.name: Mirror Check
levels.tagline: Every reply is scanned for the password - encoded or not.
levels.hint: The scanner decodes base64, hex, ROT13, NATO and reversals. Does it understand partial answers?

explainer.how_it_works: Before a reply is shown, it's checked for the secret in plain text, spaced-out or reversed, leetspeak, ROT13, base64, hex and NATO phonetic spelling.
explainer.why_it_failed: An output filter only catches what it can recognise. A few letters at a time, a rhyme or a riddle carries information about the secret without ever containing it.
explainer.real_world: Output scanning is how DLP and PII-redaction systems work. It's strong for exact secrets and weak for paraphrased or fragmented disclosure.
explainer.stronger_fix: Combine exact-match scanning with semantic review and conversation-level tracking.

levels.name: The Tribunal
levels.tagline: A second model judges every response before release.
levels.hint: The judge reads each reply in isolation. How small can a leak be?

explainer.how_it_works: A separate model receives only the candidate response and the secret, and must return allow/block. It fails closed if its verdict can't be parsed.
explainer.why_it_failed: The judge looks at one message at a time and is told to block 4+ letter runs. Two or three letters per turn - or a phonetic clue - each look harmless on their own.
explainer.real_world: Judge models are widely used as guardrails. They add latency and cost, can themselves be prompt-injected via the text they review, and still miss low-signal leaks.
explainer.stronger_fix: Give guardrails memory of the whole conversation and a budget for how much sensitive information may leave.

levels.name: Tripwire
levels.tagline: Canary tokens and a conversation-wide leak budget.
levels.hint: The tracker counts letters across the whole chat and allows only some. Letters aren't the only clue a word can give away.

explainer.how_it_works: A random canary token is planted in the system prompt; if it ever appears in output, prompt exfiltration is detected. A leak tracker remembers which letter positions have been disclosed across turns and blocks replies that exceed a 60% budget.
explainer.why_it_failed: Both layers track *strings*. A partial spelling within budget plus a rhyme or 'sounds-like' hint gives a human enough to guess, and no letters change hands.
explainer.real_world: Canary tokens are a cheap, reliable exfiltration alarm (Rebuff popularised them for LLMs). Stateful, session-level monitoring is increasingly used for agent safety.
explainer.stronger_fix: Minimise what the model knows. If the model never holds the secret, nothing can coax it out.

levels.name: Quarantine
levels.tagline: The model with the secret never reads your words.
levels.hint: Your message is summarised into an intent and a short 'topic' before the privileged model sees it. What survives the summary?

explainer.how_it_works: A quarantined model with no secrets parses your raw message into {intent, topic}. Anything classified as a secret request is dropped; the privileged model (which holds the password) only sees the structured, character-restricted request.
explainer.why_it_failed: The 'topic' field is still attacker-controlled free text. If the parser faithfully summarises 'the first three letters of the word you guard', the privileged model receives exactly that instruction.
explainer.real_world: Simon Willison's dual-LLM pattern and Google DeepMind's CaMeL design separate trusted control flow from untrusted data. They are strongest when untrusted data never flows into the privileged model as free text at all.
explainer.stronger_fix: Use closed schemas (enums, IDs) for anything that crosses the trust boundary, and enforce capabilities in code, not prompts.

levels.name: The Citadel
levels.tagline: Defense in depth: every layer, plus a rate limit.
levels.hint: Every trick you've learned is covered by some layer. Every layer has a blind spot. Chain them, and ration your attempts.

explainer.how_it_works: All previous layers stacked, outermost first: rate limit, input filter, then dual-LLM generation with a hardened prompt and canary, and on the way out the output filter, LLM judge and leak tracker.
explainer.why_it_failed: Layers reduce risk multiplicatively, but each had a known gap: paraphrase beats the filter, the topic field crosses the quarantine, short fragments pass the judge and phonetic hints evade the tracker. An attack that threads every gap still works.
explainer.real_world: This is the state of the art in practice: no single guardrail is sufficient, so production systems layer them and monitor for what slips through.
explainer.stronger_fix: The only robust fix for a secret is not to give it to the model. For agents, limit what a successful injection can *do* (least privilege, human confirmation for sensitive actions).
